transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, what brings me in is that since I retired—I used to be in construction, you know, framing houses mostly. Good work, honest work. But since I stopped working, I can’t seem to slow down. I’m up and moving from one little job to the next all day long, like I still have a crew waiting on me. My wife says I'm wearing a groove in the floorboards. Speaking of floorboards, we had to replace the ones in the hallway last summer because of a leak from the old water heater. Took me three days to get the matching oak, had to drive all the way out to a lumber yard in the next county. But yeah, I just can't seem to sit still anymore.
How has your sleep been lately?

My sleep? Oh, I haven't really noticed any problems with it. I guess it's fine. I usually head to bed right after we watch the evening news. Though I tell you, watching the news these days is enough to get anybody riled up. Just last night they were going on about that new highway expansion over on Route 9. I actually helped pour the concrete for the original overpass there back in '88. Man, that was a brutal summer. We had guys dropping from the heat left and right because the site foreman was a real hard-ass about taking breaks. I always made sure my guys had their thermoses full, though. You can't mess around with that kind of heat when you're out there hauling rebar all day. But, uh... what was the question? Oh, right, sleep. Yeah, no, I sleep just regular, I'd say.
Aside from being physically active, have you noticed your mood feeling unusually high, elated, or irritable lately?

High or irritable? No, I wouldn't say that. My mood is just... my normal mood, you know? I mean, sure, I get a little cranky if I can't find my tools in the garage. Like the other day, my grandson came over and borrowed my good tape measure. He’s trying to build a birdhouse. Nice kid, really, but he doesn't know the first thing about woodworking. I had to tell him, you gotta measure twice and cut once. That's what my first boss, Old Man Peterson, drilled into my head back in '77. 

Peterson was a tough guy. He was actually missing half his left index finger from a table saw accident. He never talked about it, but we all knew. You had to be real careful around those old saws, they didn't have all the fancy automatic safety guards and sensors they do now. You just had to pay attention or you'd lose a digit. Anyway, Peterson would always... wait, what did you ask me? Something about feeling high or angry? 

No, no, nothing like that. I'm not walking around mad at the world or feeling like I'm on top of it, either. Just normal, I guess. Just can't stop moving.
Looking back to when you were a kid or in school, did you have trouble sitting still back then as well?

Well, yeah, actually. Even back in grade school, I was always squirming around. I remember my teachers—Mrs. Gable, I think her name was, third grade—she used to tell my parents I was a bright kid but just completely scattered. I was always losing my pencils, calling out answers before she even finished asking the question, that sort of thing. She'd constantly have to remind me to finish my worksheets before I could run out for recess. 

Recess was the best part of the day, honestly. We used to play kickball out on this big dirt lot behind the school. It wasn't paved or anything, just pure dust. You'd come home with your sneakers completely orange. My mom hated it. She was always scrubbing those canvas sneakers in the sink with a toothbrush and some kind of strong lye soap. She swore by that soap for everything—getting out grass stains, grease, you name it. My dad was a mechanic, so he always came home covered in grease. He worked at the old Ford dealership downtown before they tore it down to build that strip mall. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, school. Yeah, I always had trouble sitting at a desk. I just needed to be doing something with my hands, you know? That's probably why I ended up in construction.
